claims.text: A hybrid MLIP plus selective ab initio sampling approach can accurately predict free energies and fusion properties of multicomponent high-entropy systems.
The hybrid approach can substantially reduce computational cost.
Elemental and binary systems have been validated at high temperatures.
The MLIP will be trained on ab initio molecular-dynamics data spanning both solid and fluid phases.
Active learning will update the potential in configurational regions associated with strong anharmonic and electron–vibration coupling effects.
Testing will cover temperatures from approximately 0.9 to 1.1 times the melting temperature.
Prior TOR-TILD and ab initio molecular-dynamics data exist for suitable elemental and binary benchmark systems.
The MLIP can retain key vibrational contributions in both solid and fluid phases.
The MLIP can retain key anharmonic contributions in both solid and fluid phases.
The MLIP can retain key electron–vibration coupling contributions in both solid and fluid phases.
Representative ab initio training data and active-learning refinement circumvent exhaustive full ab initio molecular-dynamics sampling across phase space.
The resulting free-energy calculations faithfully incorporate vibrational entropy and anharmonic effects.
Free energies and derived thermodynamic observables will agree with explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics results to within approximately 10% error.
The hybrid workflow will provide roughly an order-of-magnitude speed-up relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows.
The hybrid workflow will outperform TOR-TILD for multicomponent systems.
Explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows are computationally expensive.
TOR-TILD is particularly computationally expensive for high-entropy alloys.
Explicit ab initio molecular dynamics and TOR-TILD have established fidelity for elemental and simple binary systems.
The method is expected to be reliable for elemental and binary systems near fusion but is unverified outside the stated composition and temperature ranges.
The ability of the MLIP to fully capture electron–vibration coupling in complex multicomponent systems is uncertain.
